entries.title: Can something in a free game cost real money?
entries.answer: You can start some games without paying, but they may offer extra colors, characters, or game coins for sale. Some coins are earned by playing. Spending coins someone paid for still uses part of a real purchase. It can be easy to miss how many real dollars are being spent if you have already bought a pile of coins. Ask a grown-up before tapping a purchase button. Family settings can require separate approval before a sale goes through.
facts: A game can be free to start and charge separately for some extras.

entries.title: How can a password manager help a family?
entries.answer: It can be hard to remember a different long password for every account. A password manager can keep a protected list. Rather than reusing the same password on many sites, a family can use that list to keep track of separate ones. The list itself needs careful protection. Ask a grown-up before choosing or setting up a password manager, and make a family plan for keeping the things you use to open it safe.
facts: A password manager can help make a different password for each account.

entries.title: How can you spot an advertisement in a game or video?
entries.answer: An ad tries to make people interested in a product, game, or service. It can look like a separate sign. It can also fit inside a video or a game so closely that it looks like part of the fun. Look for words such as “paid” or “sponsored,” or notice when someone keeps asking you to try or buy one thing. If you cannot tell why a message is there, ask a grown-up you trust before acting on it.
facts: An ad can be part of a video or game, instead of appearing on a different screen.

entries.title: How does locking your device help protect it?
entries.answer: If you leave a tablet open, a person nearby may be able to read what you were doing or use an app that is already signed in. A device lock puts up a new check before letting someone get back to those things. A family can set a lock that needs a passcode or another way to show it is you. Locking a device when you leave it helps keep a small mistake from opening everything to someone else.
facts: A device can be set to lock when it has been left alone for a time.

entries.title: What can you do if someone is mean online?
entries.answer: If someone keeps sending mean messages or puts up something cruel about you, show a grown-up you trust. You do not have to answer or try to fix it alone. A grown-up can help decide whether to keep a record, block the person, or report what happened using the service. Forwarding a hurtful message to other players can spread the problem. Use the same care if you see someone being mean to another person online.
facts: Many games or services have settings for blocking or reporting someone.

entries.title: What counts as personal information online?
entries.answer: Personal information includes details that can identify or locate you, such as your full name or where you live. Details that seem small, like the name on a team shirt, can become revealing when someone matches them with other clues. Before putting information in a game chat or an online form, check with a grown-up you trust. You can often take part in an activity without telling everyone private facts about your family or your plans.
facts: Two small clues can reveal something that either clue alone might not reveal.

entries.title: What does privacy mean when you use a device?
entries.answer: Privacy is about how much other people can find out about you and who can see the things you share. Some games or apps let grown-ups choose whether a profile is seen by everyone or just by people they approve. Even with a private setting, someone who can see something may still copy it. Think about who needs a piece of information before you share it. A trusted grown-up can help you understand a setting while you are learning to use it.
facts: Settings may let you limit who can contact you or see a profile.

entries.title: What is a second check when you sign in?
entries.answer: Some accounts check more than one kind of proof that the person signing in is allowed. After a password, a service may ask you to approve a message on a device that belongs to you. That helps when a person knows the first secret but does not have the second proof. If someone sends you a message asking you for a sign-in code, do not share it. A trusted grown-up can help you check the request.
facts: The extra check can make it harder for someone who knows just the password to enter the account.

entries.title: What is phishing?
entries.answer: Phishing is a trick where someone makes a message look trustworthy to get you to give them something or do something. They might ask for a password, send a link that leads to a fake sign-in page, or try to get you to open a file. Some messages pretend to be from a familiar game or website. If a message surprises you or asks you to rush, stop before you tap anything. Show it to a trusted grown-up who can help check where it came from.
facts: A message can have a familiar logo and still be fake.
An unexpected request for a password is a reason to pause and ask for help.

entries.title: What should you notice before sharing a photo?
entries.answer: A picture may show more than you meant to share. Look at the background. A sign can say where you are, or a shirt can show a school name. Other people in the image might want a say too. Ask them and check with a trusted grown-up before posting. Once a picture gets shared, someone may copy it or send it on to others. Deleting your post does not necessarily remove the copies other people have.
facts: A shared photo can be copied, even if you later remove your first copy from a page.

entries.title: Why be careful with messages from people you just met online?
entries.answer: When you meet someone through a game, you may know their character name and how they play. You may know very little about who they are away from the game. If a person wants private information, asks you to move into a secret chat, or tries to get you to meet, stop the conversation and tell a trusted grown-up. You can be friendly while playing a game without sharing details or agreeing to do something away from it.
facts: People on a service can use names or pictures that are not their own.

entries.title: Why do you need a password?
entries.answer: A password is a secret you enter to help show you are allowed to sign in to an account. If someone else learns it, they may be able to sign in as you. A long password that is hard to guess helps protect the account. Using a different one on each account helps too. Then learning one password does not give someone the same secret for all your accounts. If you are setting up an account, a trusted grown-up can help you choose a password and a safe way to keep it.
facts: A familiar pet name by itself can be easy to guess.
A password manager can remember different passwords with help from its owner.

entries.title: Why does a computer ask to update?
entries.answer: An update is a newer version of part of a program or device. Sometimes it adds something people can use. Other times it repairs a problem that was there before. Some repairs protect the information on your device, even if you do not see a big change on the screen. In a family, a grown-up can use the device’s own updates or choose automatic updates. Ask before using any update mentioned in a surprising message.
facts: Some updates repair problems, even when the app looks the same after the change.

entries.title: Why does an app ask to use your camera or location?
entries.answer: An app sometimes asks to use a tool or information on your device. A family video call app may need the camera to show your face. A clock might be able to work without knowing your location. A permission is the choice about whether it can use something. When a request surprises you, you can pause and ask a grown-up you trust. The settings often let you check which permissions apps already have.
facts: Some devices let you change an app’s permission after the first choice.
